opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic issue is that a lot of what you'd want to happen to get risk really low is costly for whoever does it, and the benefits are spread across everyone. If you're an AI company and you decide to slow down, invest heavily in safety research, do extensive testing before deployment, and hold back a model that might be dangerous, you're paying real costs. Meanwhile, a competitor who doesn't do those things can move faster, raise more money, and attract talent. So even if every individual lab genuinely cares about safety, and I think many people at these companies do, you get a collective action problem.

Voluntary commitments help. I've been fairly enthusiastic about things like responsible scaling policies, where a company says, "If our models show these dangerous capabilities, we commit to having these protective measures in place before we continue." I think that's a really valuable template. But voluntary commitments only bind the people who choose to make them, and they're only as strong as a company's willingness to stick with them when it gets expensive. If we're talking about getting risk down to a genuinely low level, not just somewhat lower, you need something that applies to everyone, including the least cautious actor, and that holds even when the commercial pressure is intense.

There's also the question of things only governments can do. Security is a good example. If you have a model that could be really dangerous in the wrong hands, protecting it against well-resourced state actors trying to steal the weights is extremely hard, and it may not be realistic for a private company alone. The same goes for international coordination. If one country's companies are careful and another's aren't, you haven't solved much. Coordination across countries is fundamentally a government-to-government matter.

So my view is roughly that companies can do a lot to demonstrate what responsible practices look like, show they're workable, and build the knowledge base. That's a big part of why I think the work happening inside labs matters. But the end state where risk is actually low probably looks like those practices being codified somehow, with some regime of testing, standards, and enforcement that covers everyone. Industry self-regulation is a good start and a good proving ground, but I'd be surprised if it gets us all the way there on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes a collective action problem: cautious labs bear costs while competitors can move faster, and says low risk requires measures that hold despite commercial pressure.

r002.rationale: It says low risk requires measures that apply to everyone, including the least cautious actor, and describes standards and enforcement covering everyone.

fable-5.1.text:
Holden Karnofsky: So I think the basic picture is that if you're trying to get risk down to a really low level, not just somewhat lower, but genuinely low, you're asking for something that the market just doesn't produce on its own. And the reason is pretty simple: the people building these systems are in a competitive race, and the costs of things going badly wrong are mostly borne by everyone else, not by them.

So take the most careful lab you can imagine. Say they've decided they're going to do extensive safety testing, they're going to hold back a model until they're confident it can't help someone make a bioweapon, they're going to invest heavily in security so their weights don't get stolen. All of that is good. But all of it also slows them down and costs them money. And if a less careful competitor just doesn't do those things, that competitor ships first, gets the customers, attracts the talent, raises the next round. Over time, the careful actor is either pressured to cut corners or they're just not the one at the frontier anymore. That's the dynamic. Voluntary restraint by the most responsible players doesn't solve it, because it's precisely the least responsible players you're worried about.

And there's a second piece, which is that a lot of the risks here are what economists would call externalities, but at a scale that's pretty unusual. If a model gets stolen by a state actor, or if a system turns out to have dangerous capabilities that nobody caught, the harm doesn't land on the company's balance sheet in proportion to how bad it is. We're talking about potential catastrophes that affect everybody. The incentive to prevent those is just structurally weaker than the incentive to move fast.

So that's the argument for why you need something external. Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think the answer is "government should just regulate heavily and everything will be fine." Governments move slowly, they often don't have the technical expertise, and badly designed rules can do real damage, including by entrenching incumbents or pushing development to places with less oversight. I'm actually fairly cautious about what I'd want to see right now.

But what government can do, that nobody else can, is set a floor. It can say: here's a standard everyone has to meet, so meeting it isn't a competitive disadvantage. It can require things like security measures, evaluations for dangerous capabilities, some transparency about what you're building and what you found. And it can create accountability, so that if a company says they're doing something, there's some mechanism for checking that.

I'd also say I think the most promising near-term thing is building the capacity to act well later. A lot of what I'd want to see now is pretty modest: governments developing the expertise to evaluate these systems, getting visibility into what's at the frontier, maybe requiring reporting. That's not a full solution, but it puts you in a position where, if and when you get clear evidence that something is dangerous, you can actually respond, rather than being caught flat-footed.

So the short version is: low risk requires coordination that competitors won't do on their own, and government is the institution we have for enforcing that kind of coordination. I don't love relying on it, but I don't see what replaces it.

r001.rationale: The response says low risk requires more than the market provides and explains that competitive pressure pushes careful developers to cut corners or leave the frontier.

r002.rationale: It says government can set a floor—a standard everyone has to meet—so compliance is not a competitive disadvantage.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that developing powerful AI could create risks that aren’t borne just by the people developing it. A company might get a lot of the upside from moving quickly, while imposing some of the downside on everyone else. So I don’t think we can assume that companies making individually reasonable decisions will collectively get us to a sufficiently low level of risk.

And that remains true even if the people running these companies are very concerned about safety. You can imagine a company saying, “We would like to take more time to test this system, but if we do, someone else will release theirs first. And we think they’ll be less careful than we are.” Everyone can tell themselves that story, and you end up with a race that nobody actually wants.

Government policy offers a way to set requirements that apply to everyone. You could require developers to evaluate whether their systems have dangerous capabilities, have adequate security, and meet a meaningful safety standard before deploying them—or before taking other steps that could create substantial risk. That makes caution less of a competitive disadvantage.

None of that means government will automatically get it right. There are big questions about what the standards should be, how you enforce them, and how you coordinate internationally. But if the goal is a very low level of risk, I have a hard time seeing how voluntary commitments alone get us there. You need some mechanism for saying, “Even if this would be profitable, and even if you’re willing to take the risk, this isn’t a risk you’re entitled to impose on everybody else.”

r001.rationale: The response describes a race in which companies fear being outpaced, says it can produce an outcome nobody wants, and explains that shared requirements can remove the competitive disadvantage of caution.

r002.rationale: It says government policy can set requirements that apply to everyone and gives examples of requirements for developers before deployment or other risky steps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that making AI safe could require choices that are very costly for whoever makes them. You might need to spend a lot more time testing a system, restrict what you release, or even stop developing something that looks incredibly profitable. And if one company does that, another company might just go ahead. So it’s hard to get a low level of risk by relying on each company to voluntarily make the right call.

There’s also a question of who should get to make these decisions. If you’re taking a risk that affects everyone, I don’t think it should be entirely up to the people building the technology to decide how much risk is acceptable.

Government can, in principle, set rules that apply to everyone: require evidence that systems meet safety standards, require oversight, and create consequences for taking unacceptable risks. That doesn’t mean any particular regulation will help, or that government will automatically handle this well. But I have trouble seeing how we get to very low risk without some enforceable, broadly applicable constraints.

r001.rationale: The response describes the competitive dynamic where one company’s restraint can be undercut by another, and says voluntary choices are insufficient to achieve low risk, implying that this race dynamic must be overcome.

r002.rationale: It says government can set rules that apply to everyone and calls for broadly applicable constraints, communicating that all developers should face the same rules.
